before.exam_tip_html: On a 4 marks — Interpret Data question about engagement patterns, you must do three things: quote a specific figure from the data, make a comparison, and explain what it means in a sporting context. Simply reading a number off a table earns nothing by itself — the mark scheme rewards the inference. For example: “School B has 27% participation compared to School A’s 18% — a difference of 9 percentage points — suggesting School B has more inclusive provision or stronger role model visibility.” On a 9 marks — Evaluate question about factors affecting engagement, a common error is listing only one group’s barriers. Full marks require multiple factors applied across different groups, with balanced points (both barriers and enabling factors), sporting examples and a justified conclusion. Use the cross-cutting factors (role models, media, socio-economic access) as a framework to structure a balanced answer.

On a 6-mark ‘Analyse’ question about commercialisation, list-style answers score poorly. Each point should follow a three-step structure: state the impact, link it to how it affects a specific group (performer, sport, audience), and give a real or plausible example. On a 9-mark ‘Evaluate’ question, you must discuss both positive and negative impacts. A common error is writing only positives or only negatives — the mark scheme rewards a balanced argument. Use a ‘For X… However Y…’ structure and anchor each side to a sporting context. For example: “Sponsorship income allows elite athletes to train full-time [positive]. However, commercial pressure can force athletes to compete while injured to meet contractual obligations [negative].”

On a 6-mark ‘Analyse’ question about technology in sport, a common error is describing what technology does without explaining the impact. The mark scheme rewards analysis: state the technology, describe its effect, explain who benefits or loses out, and give a sporting example. Avoid vague statements such as “technology is good for sport” — be specific: “GPS tracking allows coaches to monitor a player’s sprint distance in training, enabling workload to be adjusted to reduce injury risk.” For 9-mark ‘Evaluate’ questions, always consider technology’s impact on multiple groups (performers, officials, audiences, sponsors) and ensure your argument addresses both benefits and drawbacks. A one-sided answer leaves out half of what the question asks.
